hints: Sort the three compounds by type: which is an acyl chloride, which is a primary chloroalkane, and which has Cl directly attached to a benzene ring?
Think about attack by water as a nucleophile on the carbon attached to Cl. How does an adjacent C=O group versus an alkyl group change the positive character on that carbon?
Recall what happens to a lone pair on Cl when it is next to a benzene pi system, and how this affects C-Cl bond strength and attack.
walkthrough:
Name the three different environments**
You are not comparing three identical $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bonds. $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ is an acyl chloride, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ is a chloroalkane, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ is a chloroarene with Cl bonded directly to the ring. Hydrolysis needs water to attack the carbon bonded to Cl, so ask how easy that carbon is to attack and how easy the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond is to break.

See why the acyl chloride is fastest**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-\text{Cl}$ the carbon is bonded to highly electronegative oxygen as $\text{C}=\text{O}$. Oxygen pulls electrons away, leaving that carbon very electron deficient and very attractive to the lone pair on water. The $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond there is also the weakest of the three, so $\text{Cl}^-$ leaves very easily. That is why acyl chlorides hydrolyse violently in cold water.

See why chlorobenzene is slowest**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ the p-orbital lone pair on Cl overlaps with the delocalised $\pi$ system of the ring. Electrons are donated into the ring, giving the $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond partial double bond character. It is shorter and stronger, and the carbon is less susceptible to nucleophilic attack. So no hydrolysis under normal conditions. The chloroalkane is in the middle: its $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ is a normal polar single bond, strengthened slightly by the positive inductive effect of the ethyl group, but with no resonance strengthening.

Final answer: Rate: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} > \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$.
$\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ is fastest as carbonyl C is strongly $\delta+$ due to attached O, and $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond is weakest.
$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ is slowest / no hydrolysis as lone pair on Cl overlaps with benzene $\pi$ system giving partial double bond character and stronger $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bond.

hints: Recall the two halves of the Bronsted-Lowry definition for a base, plus what the word weak tells you about equilibrium in water.
walkthrough:
Combine proton acceptor with partially ionised**
A base is a proton acceptor. The word weak tells you the extent. In water only a small proportion of base molecules accept a proton to form $\text{OH}^-$ and the conjugate acid, so equilibrium lies far to the left. Epibatidine therefore forms $\text{OH}^-$ to only a small extent.
Final answer: A proton acceptor that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution.

hints: Look for the two N atoms that can accept $\text{H}^+$: the bridged secondary amine and the pyridine N. What happens to each N when it reacts with $\text{HCl}$?
walkthrough:
Protonate the basic nitrogens**
Both nitrogens have a lone pair available for $\text{H}^+$. With $\text{HCl(aq)}$ each N accepts a proton. The pyridine N becomes $\text{N}^+-\text{H}$, like a pyridinium ion, and the bridged secondary amine $\text{NH}$ becomes $\text{NH}_2^+$. The product is therefore a diammonium salt, shown as the organic dication plus $2\text{Cl}^-$ ions.
Final answer: Both N atoms protonated to give dication with $2\text{Cl}^-$: pyridine $\text{N}^+-\text{H}$ and bridged $\text{NH}_2^+$ with $2\text{Cl}^-$ counter ions.

hints: Picture the two stages: water adds to $\text{C}=\text{O}$ so the $\pi$ bond breaks, then $\text{HCl}$ is eliminated as $\text{C}=\text{O}$ reforms. Which types of bond break and make overall?
walkthrough:
Track sigma and pi through addition then elimination**
Hydrolysis of $-\text{COCl}$ is addition-elimination. In step 1 water adds: the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ $\pi$ bond breaks and new $\text{C}-\text{O}$ $\sigma$ and $\text{O}-\text{H}$ changes occur. In step 2 $\text{HCl}$ is eliminated: $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ $\sigma$ breaks and $\text{C}=\text{O}$ $\pi$ reforms. Overall you both break and make $\sigma$ bonds and $\pi$ bonds, so tick both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds for broken and for formed.
Final answer: Bonds broken: both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds. Bonds formed: both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds.

hints: The monomer $\text{H}_2\text{N}-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{COCl}$ joins head to tail by amide formation with loss of $\text{HCl}$. What does the new $-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-$ link look like?

For two repeat units, write $-\text{NH}-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{CO}-$ with the amide $\text{N}-\text{H}$ and $\text{C}=\text{O}$ fully displayed and continuation bonds.
walkthrough:
Link amine end to acyl chloride end**
Think head to tail. The $\text{NH}_2$ of one monomer attacks the $\text{COCl}$ of the next, eliminating $\text{HCl}$ to give an amide $-\text{NH}-\text{CO}-$. So the backbone becomes repeating $-\text{NH}-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{CO}-$ units.

Write two units with displayed amide**
Draw two of those units joined together: $-\text{NH}-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{NH}-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{C}(=\text{O})-$. Show every atom in the amide: $\text{N}-\text{H}$ and $\text{C}$ double bonded to $\text{O}$. Put continuation bonds through the terminal $\text{N}$ and $\text{C}$ to show the polymer continues.
Final answer: $-\text{N}(\text{H})-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{N}(\text{H})-(\text{CH}_2)_5-\text{C}(=\text{O})-$ with amide bonds fully displayed and continuation bonds at each end.

hints: Divide the saturated carbon chain into pairs of adjacent carbons, each pair came from one $\text{C}=\text{C}$ monomer.
Restore the double bond in each two carbon fragment and add back the substituents seen, one fragment contains Cl and $\text{CH}_3$, the other contains alkyl groups only.
walkthrough:
Cut the chain back into alkenes**
Addition polymerisation turns each $\text{C}=\text{C}$ into a $-\text{C}-\text{C}-$ single bonded pair. To reverse it, split the given six carbon section into two carbon pairs and put the double bond back. Look at the substituents on each pair.

Identify the two different monomers**
One type of pair is $-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{Cl})-\text{CH}_2-$, which comes from $\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{Cl}$ (2-chloropropene). The other type is $-\text{CH}(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-$, which comes from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$ (pent-2-ene). Grouping the chain the other way gives the equivalent pair $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (but-1-ene) and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{Cl}$ (2-chlorobut-2-ene). Either pair is accepted.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{Cl}$ OR $\text{CH}_3\text{CCl}=\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$.

hints: Compare bond polarity: what makes the amide $\text{C}-\text{N}$ linkage open to attack by water or enzymes, while the all carbon backbone of a polyalkenes is not?
walkthrough:
Link polarity to hydrolysis**
Biodegradation usually needs hydrolysis by water or enzymes. The polyalkenes backbone is only non-polar $\text{C}-\text{C}$ and $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bonds, which water cannot attack, so it persists. Polyamides contain polar amide $\text{CO}-\text{NH}$ links which are readily hydrolysed back to acid and amine, so the chain is cut up more easily.
Final answer: $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bonds in polyalkenes are non-polar and cannot be hydrolysed, whereas polyamide linkages can be broken down by hydrolysis.

hints: Step 2 converts the ketone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ toward the alkene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ via dehydration in step 3. What alcohol must dehydrate to give that alkene?
walkthrough:
Work backwards from phenylethene**
Step 3 makes $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ from H by elimination of water, so H must be the alcohol that dehydrates to that alkene. Reduction of the methyl ketone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ gives the secondary alcohol $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$. That is compound H.
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$, 1-phenylethan-1-ol.

hints: Step 1 adds a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group to benzene by electrophilic substitution. Which acylating agent and Lewis acid catalyst are needed?
Step 2 reduces a ketone to a secondary alcohol without affecting the ring. Which mild hydride reagent is typical?
Step 3 converts the alcohol H to an alkene by elimination. What strong dehydrating acid and condition are used?
walkthrough:
Acylate benzene in step 1**
You need to put $\text{COCH}_3$ onto benzene. That is Friedel-Crafts acylation, electrophilic substitution using ethanoyl chloride $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ with the catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$ to generate the $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+\text{O}$ electrophile.

Reduce the ketone in step 2**
The ketone $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ must become the alcohol $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$. Use a hydride reducing agent such as $\text{NaBH}_4$ (or $\text{LiAlH}_4$ followed by aqueous work up). This delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon without reducing the benzene ring.

Dehydrate the alcohol in step 3**
Alcohol H eliminates water to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. Use conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with heat for acid catalysed elimination (dehydration).
Final answer: step 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} + \text{AlCl}_3$; step 2: $\text{NaBH}_4$ / $\text{LiAlH}_4$; step 3: conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat.
